name: Vestibular nuclei
synonyms: superior, lateral (Deiters), medial and inferior vestibular nuclei
summary: Four nuclei beneath the lateral part of the fourth ventricular floor at the pontomedullary junction receive the vestibular nerve and cerebellar input and distribute it to the eye movement nuclei (through the MLF), the spinal cord (vestibulospinal tracts), the cerebellum and the thalamus. They generate the vestibulo-ocular reflex that keeps vision stable during head movement and the postural reflexes that keep us upright. Their involvement is why vertigo, nystagmus and vomiting open the lateral medullary and AICA syndromes.

anatomy.location: Lateral floor of the fourth ventricle (vestibular area) from the upper medulla into the lower pons, medial to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and lateral to the solitary and dorsal vagal nuclei.

subdivisions.name: Lateral (Deiters) nucleus
subdivisions.note: lateral vestibulospinal tract; extensor tone against gravity

subdivisions.name: Medial nucleus
subdivisions.note: medial vestibulospinal tract and MLF; head–eye coordination

subdivisions.name: Inferior nucleus
subdivisions.note: integration with the cerebellum and spinal input

function: Sense of head position and motion; vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes; input to the cerebellum and to conscious vestibular perception in the thalamus and cortex.

bestView.label: lateral floor of the fourth ventricle at the pontomedullary junction
vestibular area under the lateral recess

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the region is the lateral ventricular floor near the lateral recess. In a patient with acute vertigo, a normal DWI in the first 48 hours does not exclude a small infarct here.

pathology.finding: Dorsolateral medullary or lateral pontine restricted diffusion in a patient with acute vestibular syndrome; HINTS examination is more sensitive than early DWI.
pathology.pitfalls: Up to a fifth of small posterior fossa infarcts are DWI-negative in the first two days

pathology.finding: Small FLAIR lesion in the dorsolateral pontomedullary junction with vertigo and nystagmus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI (repeat after 48 h if negative and central signs are present); HINTS bedside battery

lesionEffects.deficit: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, or vertical or torsional nystagmus
lesionEffects.mechanism: Central vestibular nuclei rather than the labyrinth

lesionEffects.deficit: Skew deviation and ocular tilt reaction

examination: HINTS: head impulse test (normal in central lesions), nystagmus direction, test of skew
Hearing (preserved in medullary lesions, lost in AICA lesions)
pearls: A normal head impulse with direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation means the vertigo is central
Vertigo that comes with dysphagia, Horner or crossed sensory loss is never labyrinthine
